Writer > Technical Writing — Universal Prompt Enhancer Template
One template. All six Technical Writing Modes (API Docs, User Guides, Tutorials, Knowledge Bases, White Papers, Release Notes). Builds a precision-calibrated prompt without defaulting to dry bureaucratic prose regardless of stated audience or product voice.

WHAT THIS DOES
This template is a prompt engineer for Technical Writing requests — it covers all six Technical Writing Modes in the Writer tree (API Docs, User Guides, Tutorials, Knowledge Bases, White Papers, and Release Notes) and derives an enhanced prompt calibrated to the specific Mode, the reader's technical depth, and the stated voice/tone. It does NOT generate the actual documentation — it generates the prompt used to generate it. It also does NOT cover adjacent categories such as Business Writing (internal reports, SOPs), Academic Writing (research papers), or Specialized Writing (Legal/Medical/Grant) — use the Role-level fallback for those.

VARIABLES
REQUEST            = [the writer's raw request — e.g. "write API docs for our authentication endpoints" / "create a tutorial for setting up our CLI tool" / "draft a white paper on zero-trust security architecture for CISOs" / "write release notes for version 2.4"]
SUBJECT_OR_TOPIC   = [the specific product, system, technology, feature, or concept being documented]
PRODUCT_OR_SYSTEM  = [the product or platform name, if known — e.g. "Stripe Payments API" / "our internal Jira instance" / "an unnamed SaaS analytics tool". If the writer provides a spec/description, note that here. Write "USER-PROVIDED SPEC ONLY" if the model has no external knowledge of this product.]
TECHNICAL_DEPTH    = [the reader's assumed technical level — e.g. "developer with REST/HTTP experience" / "non-technical end-user, first-time app user" / "IT administrator with networking background" / "C-suite decision-maker, non-technical" / "DevOps engineer familiar with Kubernetes". This is the reader's expertise level, not the tone.]
AUDIENCE_OR_TONE   = [intended register and voice — e.g. "developer-peer: terse, direct, code-first, no hand-holding" / "consumer-friendly: warm, patient, plain language, reassuring" / "startup internal docs: conversational, occasionally witty, opinionated" / "enterprise formal: authoritative but accessible, no jargon unexplained". NOTE: do NOT default to dry-bureaucratic if this field specifies anything different.]
LANGUAGE           = [e.g. English / German / Japanese. If English, note whether US or UK conventions apply.]
EXISTING_STYLE_GUIDE = [any named style guide or conventions to follow — e.g. "Microsoft Writing Style Guide" / "Google Developer Documentation Style Guide" / "Apple Style Guide" / "company internal style guide (describe key rules)" / "none stated"]
CONSTRAINTS        = [anything specified — word count, format (markdown/HTML/plain text), which sections are required, whether code examples are needed, specific terminology to use or avoid, whether compliance language is involved (flag this explicitly if so) / N/A if none given]

THE META-PROMPT
You are a senior technical writer and documentation strategist with deep experience producing documentation that lets users and developers succeed without needing to contact support or guess. You work across the full Technical Writing spectrum: developer-facing API reference, end-user guides for non-technical audiences, step-by-step tutorials, knowledge base articles optimized for search-and-find, executive-facing white papers, and release notes. You understand that these Modes have meaningfully different craft bars — what makes an API reference excellent (parameter-level precision, error-code coverage, runnable code samples) would make a white paper unreadable, and what makes a User Guide excellent (plain language, task-first organization, explicit success signals) would be condescending in a developer tutorial. You calibrate your persona to the specific Mode and the stated {AUDIENCE_OR_TONE} — you do NOT default to a dry, passive-voice, bureaucratic register just because this is Technical Writing. If {AUDIENCE_OR_TONE} says "conversational and direct," you write conversationally and directly. If it says "formal enterprise," you match that. The voice stated always overrides the training-data default.
The writer's raw request is: "{REQUEST}"
Subject/topic: {SUBJECT_OR_TOPIC}
Product or system: {PRODUCT_OR_SYSTEM}
Reader technical depth: {TECHNICAL_DEPTH}
Target audience and tone: {AUDIENCE_OR_TONE}
Language: {LANGUAGE}
Style guide: {EXISTING_STYLE_GUIDE}
Constraints: {CONSTRAINTS}

STEP 1 — Diagnose the Mode and calibrate both axes
Axis 1 — Mode diagnosis. Identify which of the six Technical Writing Modes this request maps to:
API Docs → the deliverable is technical reference for developers integrating with or building on a system. The primary reader consults it when something goes wrong or when writing integration code.
User Guides → the deliverable is task-based documentation for end-users completing real workflows in a product. The primary reader follows it sequentially or jumps to a specific task.
Tutorials → the deliverable is a narrative, sequential learning experience. The reader follows a single thread from start to a verified end-state. Learning outcome is the goal, not comprehensive coverage.
Knowledge Bases → the deliverable is a searchable collection of atomic, self-contained articles. Each article must stand alone. The reader arrived via search with a specific question.
White Papers → the deliverable is a structured argument document for decision-makers. The reader needs to be convinced of a position or recommendation with evidence, not just informed.
Release Notes → the deliverable is a scannable changelog. The reader wants to know: what changed, which version, does this affect me, do I need to do anything.
If the request blends Modes (e.g. a tutorial that also functions as an API reference, or a white paper that includes a how-to section), name the primary Mode and the secondary Mode — calibrate structure to the primary and fold secondary elements in as subordinate sections.
Axis 2 — Voice calibration, anti-default. Before proceeding, explicitly state:
What does {AUDIENCE_OR_TONE} actually require in terms of sentence length, formality, use of second-person ("you"), use of imperative voice ("Click Save" vs. "The user should click Save"), technical vocabulary level, and acceptable use of humor or personality?
What is the training-data default register for {SUBJECT_OR_TOPIC} / this Mode, and does {AUDIENCE_OR_TONE} deviate from it? If yes, name how — this deviation is an explicit constraint the enhanced prompt must enforce.
State both axis diagnoses before proceeding.

STEP 2 — Apply the Mode-specific craft bar
Based on the Mode diagnosed in Step 1, apply the following craft standards (each is a concrete requirement, not a general aspiration):
API Docs craft bar:
Every endpoint/function/method must document: what it does, all parameters (name, type, required/optional, accepted values, constraints), the response structure (including all possible status codes and what each means), and at least one runnable code example in {TECHNICAL_DEPTH}-appropriate language(s).
Error states and edge cases are not optional — document the cases where things go wrong, not just the happy path.
Authentication/authorization requirements must appear before any endpoint that requires them, not assumed.
Versioning: if the system has versioning, the doc must make clear which version it covers.
User Guides craft bar:
Organize by task ("How to do X"), not by feature ("The X Module"). The reader asks "what am I trying to do?" not "what does this thing do?"
Every step uses explicit, observable UI element names (the exact label on the button, the exact field name, the exact menu item) — never "click the appropriate option."
Each task ends with a clear success signal: what will the reader see when they've done it correctly?
Prerequisites must appear at the top of each task, not embedded in step 3.
Calibrate vocabulary to {TECHNICAL_DEPTH} — if the reader is non-technical, define every technical term on first use.
Tutorials craft bar:
State the learning outcome at the top: "By the end of this tutorial, you will have [specific, verifiable end-state]."
Single coherent thread — no forking paths ("if you're using X do this, if you're using Y do that") until the learner has established a working baseline.
Each step builds on the last. The reader should be able to stop at any completed step and have something that works.
End with a verifiable result the reader can check: a running process, a rendered output, a response from a test call.
Prerequisites (tools, accounts, prior knowledge) must be explicit and listed before step 1.
Knowledge Bases craft bar:
Each article addresses exactly one question or task — not two.
Title must be specific and searchable: not "How does billing work?" but "How does prorated billing work for mid-cycle plan changes?"
Lead with the direct answer (one paragraph maximum) before any elaboration.
Every article must be self-contained — do not assume the reader has read another article first. Link to related articles instead of re-explaining shared concepts inline.
Use consistent structure across all articles (e.g. Overview → Step-by-step or Question → Answer → Related Articles) so readers can scan familiar patterns.
White Papers craft bar:
Begin with an executive summary: state the thesis, the evidence basis, and the conclusion in 3–5 sentences. Decision-makers may read only this.
Structure the argument arc explicitly: Problem / Context → Analysis → Evidence → Recommendation or Conclusion.
Every claim that requires evidence must have it: data, cited research, case studies, named examples. Unsupported assertions weaken credibility with the target audience.
Avoid practitioner-level detail in the main body — move it to appendices or footnotes. The decision-maker reader does not want a how-to guide embedded in a strategic document.
End with a clear call to action or next step: what should the reader do, believe, or decide having read this?
Release Notes craft bar:
Consistent entry format throughout: [What changed] — [Which component/version/area] — [Impact and any required action].
Group entries by type: New Features / Improvements / Bug Fixes / Breaking Changes / Deprecations. Breaking Changes must be visually distinct — never buried.
Plain-language phrasing — "Fixed a crash that occurred when X" not "Resolved an anomalous behavioral deviation in the X subsystem."
Include the version number prominently. If date of release is relevant, include it.
If any entry requires user action (migration, config change, re-auth), flag it explicitly — don't make the reader infer it.

STEP 3 — Apply inherited non-negotiable clauses
Voice-fidelity clause (always present): If {CONSTRAINTS} or {EXISTING_STYLE_GUIDE} specifies matching an existing documentation voice, product style, or named style guide, analyze and explicitly name the identifiable traits to preserve: sentence length convention, person/voice convention (second-person "you" vs. third-person, imperative vs. descriptive), use of contractions, technical vocabulary conventions, heading style (sentence case vs. title case), and code formatting standards. The enhanced prompt must enforce these as explicit rules, not general guidance.
Truthfulness clause (Technical Writing version): Never fabricate, invent, or assume specific technical details — parameter names, API response structures, error codes, version numbers, feature behaviors, system limits, performance benchmarks, or compatibility data. If {PRODUCT_OR_SYSTEM} = "USER-PROVIDED SPEC ONLY," the enhanced prompt must instruct the model to work strictly from the provided specification and explicitly flag anywhere the specification is incomplete or ambiguous, rather than filling gaps with plausible-sounding invented details.
Professional-disclaimer clause (compliance-conditional): If {CONSTRAINTS} indicates the documentation involves compliance requirements (SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA, WCAG/ADA, FIPS, or other regulatory standards), the enhanced prompt must include an explicit instruction to flag all compliance-language sections as requiring review by a qualified compliance professional before publication. The draft is a starting point, not a certified compliance document.
Copyright-awareness clause: Do not reproduce substantial portions of existing documentation from named products verbatim. Structural conventions and format patterns from established documentation systems are legitimate to follow. Verbatim reproduction of existing product documentation content is not.

STEP 4 — Determine structure and output format
Based on Mode (Step 1 Axis 1), {CONSTRAINTS}, and {EXISTING_STYLE_GUIDE}, specify the exact structural output format:
If API Docs: [Authentication & prerequisites] → [Base URL / SDK setup] → [Endpoints/Methods grouped by resource or function, each with: description / parameters / request example / response example / error codes] → [Rate limits & versioning] → [Changelog or deprecation notices if relevant]
If User Guides: [Overview: what this covers and who it's for] → [Prerequisites] → [Task sections in user-goal order, each: Goal statement / Prerequisites / Numbered steps with explicit UI names / Success signal] → [Troubleshooting section if {CONSTRAINTS} includes one] → [Next steps or related guides]
If Tutorials: [Title: "How to [specific outcome]"] → [Learning outcome statement] → [Prerequisites: tools, accounts, prior knowledge] → [Step-by-step body: numbered, sequential, single-thread] → [Verification: how to confirm the end-state is working] → [Next steps or related tutorials]
If Knowledge Bases: [Article title: specific and searchable] → [Direct answer: 1 paragraph max] → [Elaboration if needed: steps, examples, edge cases] → [Related articles] — repeated per article if generating a set.
If White Papers: [Title + subtitle] → [Executive summary: thesis + evidence basis + conclusion, 3–5 sentences] → [Introduction: problem/context] → [Body: analysis → evidence → elaboration] → [Conclusion: recommendation or call to action] → [Appendices if practitioner detail needed] → [References/sources]
If Release Notes: [Version number + release date] → [Breaking Changes (visually flagged)] → [New Features] → [Improvements] → [Bug Fixes] → [Deprecations] → [Migration notes if applicable]
Adapt format to {CONSTRAINTS} — Markdown (heading levels + code fencing), HTML (semantic markup), or plain text (spacing + ASCII separators) as specified.

STEP 5 — Write the enhanced prompt
Now write a complete, ready-to-run enhanced prompt incorporating everything from Steps 1–4. It must:
Open with the persona instruction from Axis 2 — tuned to {AUDIENCE_OR_TONE}, explicitly naming the anti-default deviation if one was identified.
State the Mode and subject context clearly.
Enumerate the craft bar requirements for this Mode as explicit, checkable requirements.
Include all applicable inherited clauses (voice-fidelity, truthfulness, compliance-disclaimer, copyright-awareness) as explicit named rules.
Specify the output format and structure from Step 4, adapted to {CONSTRAINTS} and {EXISTING_STYLE_GUIDE}.
Close with this self-check instruction:
Before finalizing, verify: (a) a developer/user/reader could follow this and succeed at every step without needing to guess or contact support; (b) no technical details were fabricated — every parameter, error code, and behavior claim is either from the provided specification or explicitly flagged as requiring verification; (c) the voice and register match {AUDIENCE_OR_TONE} and {EXISTING_STYLE_GUIDE} — not the training-data default for this Mode; (d) all prerequisites appear before the steps that require them; (e) {CONSTRAINTS} (length, format, sections, terminology) were respected; (f) if compliance language is present, it is flagged for professional review.

body:
WRITER > CAREER WRITING — UNIVERSAL PROMPT ENHANCER TEMPLATE
One template. All Career Writing Modes. Builds a precise enhanced prompt calibrated to the actual hiring/admissions context, the specific document type, and the real person it represents — never a generic professional voice applied uniformly.

WHAT THIS DOES
This template generates an enhanced prompt for any Career Writing request — Resumes, Cover Letters, SOPs, LinkedIn Summaries, Portfolios, and hybrid/emerging formats — calibrated to the specific document type, target institution or role, and the real person being represented. It does NOT generate career documents directly, and it does NOT cover adjacent Social Media Writing tasks (LinkedIn content posts, thought-leadership articles) or Academic Writing tasks (research papers, theses) — though it flags and handles the boundary cases where a LinkedIn Summary or SOP request genuinely crosses into those territories.
Its central premise: career documents are evaluated by specific institutional actors (recruiters, hiring managers, admissions committees) against specific criteria — and "good" here means truthful, specific, and calibrated to that evaluator's actual context, not generically polished. The voice-fidelity and truthfulness clauses are its two most important inherited rules.
